recent_posts.title: Returning several values from a function in C++ (C++23 edition) – Daniel Lemire's blog
recent_posts.summary: C++ has evolved to provide flexible solutions for returning multiple values from functions. Using std::pair and std::tuple allows returning several values, while structured bindings enhance readability. C++23 introduces std::expected for better error handling, offering an alternative to std::optional, which is less suited for passing error messages. These techniques improve code readability and maintainability.

recent_posts.title: C++20 concepts for nicer compiler errors – Daniel Lemire's blog
recent_posts.summary: C++20 introduces concepts, a mechanism to define and enforce constraints on template parameters, improving the clarity of compiler error messages. They allow developers to specify requirements like copyability and destructibility, helping catch mismatches early and making code more expressive. Concepts aim to enhance readability and usability of C++ templates, known for generating complex error messages.

recent_posts.title: How can really smart people appear totally incompetent? – Daniel Lemire's blog
recent_posts.summary: Highly competent people and organizations often appear dysfunctional because their true objectives may differ from what they publicly claim. Examples include universities providing poor educational experiences, companies like Apple and Intel underperforming despite past successes, and institutions engaging in deceptive practices. A culture of lies about objectives can lead to significant dysfunctions.

recent_posts.title: How helpful is AI? – Daniel Lemire's blog
recent_posts.summary: AI tools can significantly enhance productivity depending on the complexity of the task. For routine tasks, AI might make you 10x faster, but for highly specialized work, its impact is minimal. Highly skilled individuals can benefit significantly by automating boilerplate tasks, potentially increasing their productivity further.

recent_posts.title: Faster shuffling in Go with batching – Daniel Lemire's blog
recent_posts.summary: Using batching techniques to generate random numbers can significantly speed up the shuffling of large data sets in Go, achieving performance improvements of over 2x compared to the standard rand.Shuffle method. This involves generating multiple random numbers from a single 64-bit value. Code examples and benchmarks are provided to illustrate these enhancements.

recent_posts.title: Mixing ARM NEON with SVE code for fun and profit – Daniel Lemire's blog
recent_posts.summary: ARM processors in mobile devices and servers support special instructions like ARM NEON for parallelism using SIMD. More recent ARM processors also support advanced instructions called SVE (Scalable Vector Extension) and its updates (SVE 2 and SVE 2.1). Mixing ARM NEON with SVE can enhance efficiency, allowing tasks to be accomplished with fewer instructions. Functions like svset_neonq and svget_neonq help convert between NEON and SVE vectors, optimizing performance on processors that support these extensions.

recent_posts.title: Unsigned comparisons using signed types – Daniel Lemire's blog
recent_posts.summary: Fixed-precision integers are typically represented as either unsigned or signed. In C++20, signed integers must use two’s complement representation, which allows efficient arithmetic operations on both positive and negative values. This method uses the leftmost bit as the sign bit and involves flipping bits and adding one to represent negative numbers. Comparisons between signed types can be conducted as if they were unsigned by adjusting values correctly.

recent_posts.title: Speeding up C++ code with template lambdas – Daniel Lemire's blog
recent_posts.summary: Learn how to speed up C++ code using template lambdas. By turning a divisor parameter into a compile-time constant using template functions, significant performance improvements can be achieved. Combining this with lambda functions keeps your code cleaner and more efficient.

recent_posts.title: An overview of parallel programming (Go edition) – Daniel Lemire's blog
recent_posts.summary: Concurrency in software development enables programs to utilize multiple processors effectively. This post covers the complexities and strategies of handling concurrency in Go, focusing on goroutines, channels, and synchronization techniques such as WaitGroups, atomic operations, and mutexes. It highlights the trade-offs in performance and complexity when using parallelism, and provides examples to illustrate how different synchronization methods are implemented in Go to avoid data races and ensure thread safety.

recent_posts.title: How fast can you open 1000 files? – Daniel Lemire's blog
recent_posts.summary: Jarred Sumner noted on X that macOS has slow file opening due to thread contention. Daniel Lemire tested this by writing a C++ program to open 1000 files using varying thread counts on an Apple M2 laptop and a big x64 Linux server. Results showed macOS is slower despite better hardware, while Linux performed better overall. More threads didn't always mean better performance, and thread pools sometimes helped on the bigger machine.
